The speaker announced Labor's opposition to the national rollout of the cashless debit card, but supported extending existing trials in Ceduna, East Kimberley, and Goldfields until June 2020 to avoid disruption. Labor will move an amendment allowing people to leave the card if they demonstrate responsible financial management, and criticised the government for relying on the flawed ORIMA evaluation.

The bill extends the cashless debit card program in Ceduna, East Kimberley, and Goldfields, and income management in Cape York, for one year until 30 June 2020, citing reductions in alcohol, drug, and gambling abuse. The member for Grey was thanked for his support of the Ceduna trial site.

The speaker argued that the cashless debit card rollout is unfair and lacks evidence, and supported Labor’s amendments—accepted by the government—to allow participants to opt out, calling for community‑controlled, evidence‑based approaches.
Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management and Cashless Welfare) Act 2019

The bill would let the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation finance more overseas infrastructure projects that benefit Australia.
It would give Efic a new power to back projects based on an Australian benefit test and raise its callable capital by $1 billion.
Efic could also operate under the trading name Export Finance Australia.
Increases Efic's callable capital by $1 billion.
Grants Efic a new overseas infrastructure financing power.
Allows Efic to use the trading name Export Finance Australia.
The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation and Australian businesses involved in regional infrastructure projects.

The majority voted in favour of the main idea of the bill, which means the Senate can now discuss it in more detail. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What does the bill do? The bill [was introduced to](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6263): > *expand the ability of the [Export Finance and Insurance Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_Finance_and_Insurance_Corporation) to finance infrastructure projects by increasing its [callable capital](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/callable-capital) and granting it a new overseas infrastructure financing power.*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2019-04-03.217.1) to pass the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6263) in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). Since the bill was already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does this bill do? The bill was introduced to: > *expand the ability of the [Export Finance and Insurance Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Export_Finance_and_Insurance_Corporation) to finance infrastructure projects by increasing its callable capital and granting it a new overseas infrastructure financing power.*

The opposition supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which provides Efic with an extra $1 billion in callable capital, renames it Export Finance Australia, and introduces an Australian benefits test for loans funding Pacific infrastructure; the bill was referred to a Senate inquiry reporting by 26 March 2019. The speech noted bipartisan backing, citing Bill Shorten's proposed Pacific infrastructure investment bank and the government's $2 billion Australian Infrastructure Financing Facility for the Pacific, and suggested examining the US BUILD Act and UK CDC Group as alternative models.

The bill provides the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation with an additional $1 billion in capital for commercial infrastructure loans in the Pacific, subject to an Australian benefit test. The speaker also criticised the coalition government for neglecting Pacific relations, particularly through climate change inaction and $11 billion in aid cuts.

The speaker argued that Australia should support Pacific infrastructure through the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill 2019, providing an additional $1 billion in callable capital for loans on a commercial basis, to boost regional prosperity, security, and economic integration while also benefiting Australian exporters like those in Tasmania.

The speaker argued that the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment Bill is welcome but overdue, and criticised the government for failing to take the Pacific seriously, citing the Prime Minister's absence from the September Pacific Islands Forum, Environment Minister Melissa Price's reported "chequebook" comment to former Kiribati president Anote Tong, and the agriculture visa debacle, while supporting the Seasonal Worker Program and calling for a credible climate change policy.

The speaker supported the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019, which renames Efic to Export Finance Australia and provides an extra $1 billion in callable capital for infrastructure financing in the Pacific, including East Timor, with a new Australian benefits test replacing the previous one-third Australian content requirement. The speaker noted bipartisan agreement on Pacific funding, referenced the opposition leader’s October 2018 announcement and the Prime Minister’s subsequent similar announcement, and called for Senate committee scrutiny to address concerns about project quality and unintended consequences.

The speaker expressed concerns about the bill's $1 billion increase in callable capital for Efic and the lack of accompanying policy frameworks, noted Labor's prior proposal for a government-backed infrastructure investment bank, and criticised the government for cutting $11 billion in development assistance over five years.

The Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Bill 2019 received bipartisan support to enhance Australia's infrastructure investment in the Pacific, with Efic to operate under the trading name Export Finance Australia.

The Greens moved an amendment to prohibit the Export Finance and Insurance Corporation (Efic) from funding or facilitating thermal coal mining and export on a commercial scale, including projects like the Adani coalmine, and criticised the government for secretly altering Efic's mandate in 2017 to allow coal funding.
Export Finance and Insurance Corporation Amendment (Support for Infrastructure Financing) Act 2019

The Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill 2018 creates a new tower access regime allowing emergency services like police, fire and ambulance to access NBN Co towers, and permits the Minister for Communications to designate temporary towers as low-impact facilities; it also includes minor technical amendments to transmitter licence refunds and broadcasting support payments.

The speaker supported the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill 2018, including its schedules to streamline temporary mobile tower deployment and require NBN Co to provide emergency services access to its towers, and noted a Labor amendment to specify Network Investments Pty Ltd as eligible for transitional support payments previously intended for Northern Rivers Television Pty Ltd.

Labor supported Schedules 1 and 2 of the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill 2018, which extend immunities from local planning laws for temporary mobile towers during natural disasters and emergencies. The party also highlighted a $250 million regional backbone blackspots program initiated under Labor, criticised the government's management of the program, and noted an amendment to permit Northern Rivers Television Pty Ltd to receive transitional support payments.

The speaker argued for passage of the Telecommunications Legislation Amendment Bill 2018, which creates a tower access regime for NBN Co, allows the minister to designate temporary towers as low-impact facilities, and requires NBN Co to provide emergency services with tower access on a non-discriminatory basis, while also addressing committee recommendations and including technical amendments to transmitter licence refunds and broadcasting support payments.

Amends the Passenger Movement Charge Collection Act to allow regulations for charging and recovering fees related to the passenger movement charge.
Unlawful non-citizens subject to removal, the Department of Home Affairs, persons entitled to recoverable payments, and entities paying or dealing with the passenger movement charge.

Returned from the House of Representatives

The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act to allow return of unlawful noncitizens without a visa in more circumstances, such as transit refusal or UN Human Rights Committee interim measures, and clarifies that visa application bars continue as if they never left. It also enables document delivery via online accounts, inserts a power to refund duty when overpaid, recovers merchant fees for credit card payments, and makes minor technical amendments to the Customs Act.

The speech supported the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 while accusing the Minister for Home Affairs of mismanagement. It cited partner visa processing times rising from 19 to 30 months for 90% of applications, more than 176,000 bridging visas, and an ANAO report finding only two of 33 consultant contracts were evaluated.

The Greens argued the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 contains provisions that bar asylum seekers returned to Australia after a third country refuses them from reapplying for protection, which the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights flagged as a human rights concern. The Greens will further examine the bill in the Senate and do not support it.

The Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018 amends the Migration Act 1958, Customs Act 1901, and Passenger Movement Charge Collection Act 1978. Key changes include allowing unlawful noncitizens returned to Australia after a failed removal to re-enter without a visa, permitting the Department of Home Affairs to use ImmiAccount for legal communications, enabling recoverable customs payments, controlling movement between sea installations and the coast, regulating disposal of narcotic-related goods, and prescribing fees for passenger movement charge collection.

The government moved to reject Senate amendments to the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment Bill, arguing they would unconstitutionally increase public expenditure from standing appropriations by requiring the minister to appoint at least six doctors to a health panel. The speaker claimed Labor had supported the amendments in December 2018 without security agency advice, then withdrew support months later, and warned that accepting the amendments would breach 109 years of House of Representatives practice and section 53 of the Constitution by allowing the Senate to initiate spending.

The speaker moved an amendment to set aside constitutional disputes with the Senate over the Home Affairs Legislation Amendment (Miscellaneous Measures) Bill 2018, citing public interest in speedy passage, and noted that the Howard government had moved an identical resolution in November 1996.

The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 introduces an assessable sponsorship framework for family sponsored visas, requiring sponsors to be assessed and approved before a visa application can proceed, with character checks shared with applicants. The bill aims to protect vulnerable visa applicants from domestic violence by allowing refusal or cancellation of sponsorship for sponsors with violent histories, initially applying to partner visas.

Labor supported the Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016, which introduces an assessable sponsorship framework for family visas, allowing refusal or cancellation of sponsors with a history of family violence. The party urged the government to create a new temporary visa with work rights for people on temporary visas fleeing domestic violence.

The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 strengthens the Migration Act to reduce family violence, including requiring pre-approval of sponsors for family stream visa applications and allowing character check results to be shared with the sponsored person. The amendments support the second action plan of the National Plan to Reduce Violence against Women and their Children 2010-2022.

Labor opposed the amendments to the Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016, arguing they assign financial responsibility for health costs to sponsored family visa holders with no guarantee the debt recovery function would not extend beyond parent visas, and that the government broke its election promise by failing to protect children and migrant communities.

The Migration Amendment (Family Violence and Other Measures) Bill 2016 was introduced to extend the assessable sponsorship framework to family sponsored visas, replacing unenforceable undertakings with statutory obligations enforced by civil penalties and administrative sanctions. The framework requires sponsor approval before visa applications, enables refusal, cancellation or barring of sponsors for family violence, and improves information sharing.
